Mixed graphical models

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/mixed-graphical-models.Rmd
mixed-graphical-models.Rmd

Studies in psychology and education often measure variables of different types together: continuous scale scores such as motivation or self-efficacy alongside binary variables such as a diagnosis, a passed course or a reported behaviour. A Gaussian graphical model requires every variable to be continuous and an Ising model requires every variable to be binary, so neither can place both kinds in one network without transforming some of them. A mixed graphical model (Haslbeck & Waldorp, 2020) does. Each variable is regressed on all the others with a model suited to its type, linear for continuous and logistic for binary variables, and the regression coefficients form the edges. An edge is an association that remains with all other variables held constant; a missing edge means that the association is accounted for by the rest of the network.

This article estimates a mixed network of three continuous and two binary indicators of self-regulated learning, reads its edges, describes the nodes by centrality and by type-appropriate predictability, and examines how the rule that combines the two regressions of each pair changes the result.

library(psychnets)

Data

SRL_GPT holds 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire. The responses were generated by a large language model (GPT) in a study of how such models answer psychological surveys (Saqr, 2025); they serve as a well-structured example and are not evidence about students. To obtain variables of both types, two of the five construct scores are recoded as binary indicators.

  • Continuous nodes: CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value) and SE (self-efficacy), construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7.
  • Binary nodes: SR_hi, 1 when self-regulation is at or above its median; TA_hi, 1 when test anxiety is at or above its median.
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.
mixed_data <- transform(SRL_GPT,
                        SR_hi = as.integer(SR >= median(SR)),
                        TA_hi = as.integer(TA >= median(TA)),
                        SR = NULL, TA = NULL)
head(mixed_data)
#>        CSU       IV       SE SR_hi TA_hi
#> 1 5.307692 5.666667 5.777778     0     1
#> 2 5.846154 6.444444 6.000000     1     1
#> 3 6.615385 6.666667 6.222222     1     0
#> 4 5.692308 6.555556 6.333333     1     1
#> 5 4.384615 5.555556 4.888889     0     1
#> 6 4.846154 5.444444 5.666667     0     0

The recoding is for illustration. In an applied study a continuous variable is kept continuous unless its two states have a substantive meaning.

The model

A mixed graphical model is a pairwise Markov random field,

p(x1,…,xp)∝exp⁡(∑jϕj(xj)+∑j<kϕjk(xj,xk)), p(x_1, \ldots, x_p) \propto \exp\left(\sum_j \phi_j(x_j) + \sum_{j<k}\phi_{jk}(x_j, x_k)\right),

in which a zero pairwise term ϕjk\phi_{jk} means that xjx_j and xkx_k are independent given all other variables. It is estimated one node at a time: for node jj, the coefficients 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta minimize

1n∑i=1nℓ(xij,β0+𝐱i,−j𝖳𝛃)+λj‖𝛃‖1, \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell\left(x_{ij}, \beta_0 + \mathbf{x}_{i,-j}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta\right) + \lambda_j\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1 ,

where ℓ\ell is the Gaussian or binomial negative log-likelihood and the ℓ1\ell_1 penalty sets weak coefficients to zero. The penalty λj\lambda_j is chosen for each node by the extended BIC (γ=0.25\gamma = 0.25 by default), and selected coefficients below a small threshold that shrinks with the sample size are then set to zero (threshold = "LW", as in mgm). Continuous variables are standardized, so their units do not determine the coefficients. Each pair then has two estimates, one from each regression. The AND rule keeps the pair when both regressions select it, the OR rule when either does, and the edge weight is the mean of the two estimates.

Node types are detected from the data: factor and character columns, and numeric columns with at most 10 distinct integer values, are categorical, and other numeric columns are Gaussian. Here the two 0/1 indicators are binary and the three scores Gaussian. When the integer rule turns a numeric column into a categorical node, a warning names it; the types argument overrides the detection.

Which variables are directly associated?

psychnet() with method = "mgm" estimates the network with the AND rule.

mixed_net <- psychnet(data = mixed_data, method = "mgm")
summary(mixed_net)
#> <psychnet> mgm network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 6   (undirected)
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 5.00e-11
#>   edge weight: range [0.196, 0.632], mean 0.413
as.data.frame(mixed_net)
#>   from    to    weight
#> 1  CSU    IV 0.5179205
#> 2  CSU    SE 0.4850679
#> 3   IV    SE 0.1970362
#> 4  CSU SR_hi 0.4509658
#> 5   IV SR_hi 0.6323683
#> 6   SE SR_hi 0.1956633

The network has 6 edges, all positive, with weights from 0.196 to 0.632. The strongest joins intrinsic value and high self-regulation (0.632): with the other variables held constant, respondents with higher intrinsic value are more likely to be in the upper half of self-regulation. Cognitive strategy use is joined to intrinsic value (0.518), self-efficacy (0.485) and high self-regulation (0.451). High test anxiety has no edge: under the AND rule, no pair involving it is selected by both of its regressions.

Edge weights are on different scales for continuous–continuous, continuous–binary and binary–binary pairs, so magnitudes are compared within a pair type. For a binary–binary edge, the sign of the logistic coefficient is kept; some software reports only its magnitude, because that sign depends on how the categories are coded.

Is the fitted network the optimum of its objective?

Each penalized regression is solved iteratively. Any solution must satisfy the problem’s optimality (Karush–Kuhn–Tucker) conditions; the amount by which a fitted network violates them, the largest over the nodewise regressions, is its certificate, and a value near zero shows that the network is the optimum of its objective.

certificate(mixed_net)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1    mgm 4.997067e-11  kkt      TRUE

The violation is 5.00×10−115.00 \times 10^{-11}, so the edges are the solutions of the penalized regressions. The certificate concerns the computation, not the sampling stability of the edges or the measurement of the variables.

Which variables are most connected?

net_centralities() returns strength, the sum of absolute edge weights, and expected influence, the signed sum.

net_centralities(mixed_net)
#>    node  strength expected_influence
#> 1   CSU 1.4539542          1.4539542
#> 2    IV 1.3473249          1.3473249
#> 3    SE 0.8777674          0.8777674
#> 4 SR_hi 1.2789974          1.2789974
#> 5 TA_hi 0.0000000          0.0000000

Cognitive strategy use has the largest strength (1.454), followed by intrinsic value (1.347) and high self-regulation (1.279). All edges are positive, so expected influence equals strength, and high test anxiety has 0 on both. Because the edge scales differ by pair type, centrality compares the continuous and binary nodes only roughly.

How well is each variable predicted by the others?

Predictability uses a measure suited to each node type: R2R^2 for continuous nodes, and for binary nodes the normalized classification accuracy, nCC⁡j=(CC⁡j−mj)/(1−mj)\operatorname{nCC}_j = (\operatorname{CC}_j - m_j)/(1 - m_j), where CC⁡j\operatorname{CC}_j is the proportion classified correctly and mjm_j the proportion in the larger category (Haslbeck & Waldorp, 2018). net_predict() needs the data to compute both.

net_predict(mixed_net, data = mixed_data)
#>    node     type metric predictability accuracy
#> 1   CSU gaussian     R2      0.8131079       NA
#> 2    IV gaussian     R2      0.7757368       NA
#> 3    SE gaussian     R2      0.7153497       NA
#> 4 SR_hi   binary    nCC      0.7391304     0.88
#> 5 TA_hi   binary    nCC      0.0000000     0.50

The other variables explain 81% of the variance in cognitive strategy use (R2=0.813R^2 = 0.813), 78% in intrinsic value and 72% in self-efficacy. High self-regulation is classified correctly for 88% of the respondents, an nCC of 0.739 over its base rate. High test anxiety has nCC = 0 and 50% correct: with no edges, it is predicted no better than by its base rate. These are in-sample values.

Does the edge-combination rule change the network?

The two regressions of a pair can disagree. With rule = "OR" a pair is kept when either regression selects it.

mixed_or <- psychnet(data = mixed_data, method = "mgm", rule = "OR")
summary(mixed_or)
#> <psychnet> mgm network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 7   (undirected)
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 5.00e-11
#>   edge weight: range [-0.168, 0.632], mean 0.330
as.data.frame(mixed_or)
#>    from    to     weight
#> 1   CSU    IV  0.5179205
#> 2   CSU    SE  0.4850679
#> 3    IV    SE  0.1970362
#> 4   CSU SR_hi  0.4509658
#> 5    IV SR_hi  0.6323683
#> 6    SE SR_hi  0.1956633
#> 7 SR_hi TA_hi -0.1681336

The OR network has 7 edges: the six AND edges with the same weights and a negative edge between high self-regulation and high test anxiety (-0.168). Respondents in the upper half of self-regulation are less likely to be in the upper half of test anxiety, with the continuous constructs held constant, but only one of the two regressions supports this association. It is the edge through which test anxiety connects to the network, and it is reported as dependent on the combination rule. The other six edges are selected under either rule.

What does the network look like?

cograph::splot() draws the network, with green positive and red negative edges and a ring showing each node’s predictability.

cograph::splot(mixed_net, psych_styling = TRUE, predictability = TRUE)

The figure shows four connected nodes and an isolated high test anxiety node with an empty predictability ring. Node positions come from a layout algorithm and carry no statistical meaning.

Reporting the analysis

A report identifies each node as continuous or binary, defines the binary coding, and states the sample size, γ\gamma, the combination rule and the treatment of missing data. Edge weights are reported numerically, and predictability with the measure matching each node type.

In this analysis, a mixed graphical model of three continuous and two binary nodes from 300 complete responses kept 6 positive edges under the AND rule, the largest between intrinsic value and high self-regulation (0.632), and left high test anxiety isolated. Under the OR rule a seventh, negative edge joined high self-regulation and high test anxiety (-0.168).

Assumptions and when to use a mixed graphical model

  • The model is for data that combine continuous and binary variables. With continuous variables only, a Gaussian graphical model is simpler; with binary variables only, the Ising model.
  • Continuous nodes are modelled by linear regression, binary nodes by logistic regression, and observations are independent of one another.
  • Categorical variables with more than two levels require native = FALSE, which fits a multinomial regression through the optional glmnet package and keeps the variable as one node. One-hot coding is not an equivalent alternative, because it turns one variable into several nodes.
  • Edges selected only under the OR rule are less certain than those selected under both rules.
  • Edges are conditional associations, not causal effects.

References

Haslbeck, J. M. B., & Waldorp, L. J. (2018). How well do network models predict observations? On the importance of predictability in network models. Behavior Research Methods, 50(2), 853-861. doi:10.3758/s13428-017-0910-x

Haslbeck, J. M. B., & Waldorp, L. J. (2020). mgm: Estimating time-varying mixed graphical models in high-dimensional data. Journal of Statistical Software, 93(8), 1-46. doi:10.18637/jss.v093.i08

Saqr, M. (2025). Delving into the psychology of machines: Exploring the structure of self-regulated learning via LLM-generated survey responses. Computers in Human Behavior, 173, 108769. doi:10.1016/j.chb.2025.108769
